questions.p: Which statement best describes data communication?
o: The exchange of information between two devices through a transmission medium
That is the slide’s definition: two devices, information exchanged, a medium in between.
The storage of information on a device so that it can be read later
Storing data isn’t exchanging it. Data communication needs a sender, a receiver and a medium between them.
A set of rules that two devices must follow
That defines a protocol, which is one component of data communication, not the whole thing.
A group of devices connected by links
That defines a network. Data communication is the exchange between two devices.

questions.p: Which of these is a transmission medium?
o: A medium is the physical path the signal travels on: copper, fibre or air.
A router is a networking device (a node), not the path between devices.
TCP/IP is a protocol suite, a set of rules, not a physical path.
That is the message, the information being sent.

questions.p: The __ is the physical path over which a message travels.
o: The transmission medium is the physical path: cable, fibre or air.
A protocol is the set of rules for communicating, not the path the signal takes.
This sounds right in plain English, but it is not one of the five components; the component is called the medium.
The signal is what travels along the medium, not the path itself.

questions.p: Which is NOT one of the five components of a data communication system?
o: The five are message, sender, receiver, transmission medium and protocol. A router is a networking device used in larger networks.
The protocol is a component: the rules both sides follow.
The message is a component: it is the information being sent.
The receiver is a component: the device that gets the message.

questions.p: Two devices are connected by a working cable but cannot understand each other’s data. Which component is missing?
o: The cable is working, so the medium is present.
There is a device receiving the data; it just doesn’t follow the same rules.
The medium connects them, but without the same rules on both sides the data can’t be interpreted.
Data is being sent, so there is a message; it just can’t be understood.

questions.p: Text is represented in data communication as:
o: A bit pattern using a code such as Unicode
Each character gets a code number, which is sent as bits.
That describes audio before it is digitised.
That is how images are represented.

questions.p: Video is represented as:
o: A single bit pattern using Unicode
That is how numbers are represented.
A series of images shown in rapid succession
Video is many still images shown quickly, each one a bit pattern.

questions.p: Numbers are converted to binary before they are sent.
o: The slide says numbers are represented in binary.
The statement is true: numbers are sent in binary, while text uses a code like Unicode.

questions.p: Frequency of failure and recovery time after a failure measure a network’s:
o: Feasibility isn’t one of the three network criteria at all.
Performance is measured by throughput and delay, not by failures.
Reliability is how dependable the network is: how often it fails and how quickly a link recovers.
Security is about protecting data from unauthorised access and damage.

questions.p: Network performance is evaluated by:
o: The slide lists throughput (data a user can send) and delay (transit and response time).
The number of users affects performance, but it isn’t how performance is measured.

questions.p: Increasing throughput usually also increases delay.
o: More data entering the network means more queuing, so delay goes up. That is why the two goals pull against each other.
The statement is true. More throughput means more data in the network, which raises the delay; the slide says the two contradict each other.

questions.p: Which is a host rather than a networking device?
o: The slide lists the modem as a networking device.
A router is a networking device that moves data between networks.
A switch is a networking device that connects devices in a LAN.
A host is a device people use: computer, printer, phone.

questions.p: A link that is shared by more than two devices is a:
o: Full-duplex describes the direction of data flow, not how many devices share the link.
Mesh uses many dedicated point-to-point links.
Point-to-point is a dedicated link between exactly two devices.
Multipoint means one link shared by more than two devices.

questions.p: A company adds firewalls and a plan for restoring data after a breach. Which network criterion is it improving?
o: Topology is the layout of the network, not a criterion.
Performance is speed: throughput and delay.
Reliability is about failures and recovery of links, not breaches.
Protecting data and having recovery policies for breaches is security.

questions.p: A point-to-point connection can be wireless.
o: The figure shows a satellite link between two stations. What matters is that the link is dedicated to two devices, not whether it is a cable.
The statement is true: the slide shows a wireless point-to-point link. Point-to-point is about two devices having the link to themselves.

questions.p: A TV remote control and its television communicate over:
o: The infrared link joins exactly two devices and nobody else uses it.
Multipoint needs more than two devices sharing the link.
A bus is a shared backbone cable for many devices.

questions.p: In a __ connection, more than two devices can share a single link.
o: Primary is a station role in some protocols, not a connection type.
Multipoint is the one where a single link is shared by more than two devices.
Point-to-point is dedicated to exactly two devices.
Secondary is a station role, not a connection type.

questions.p: In a multipoint connection, the devices take turns using the full capacity of the link. This kind of sharing is:
o: Simplex is one-way data flow, not a way of sharing a link.
Spatial sharing means several devices use the link at the same time.
Taking turns over time is temporal sharing.
Dedicated is the opposite of shared.

questions.p: In full-duplex transmission, both stations can transmit and receive simultaneously.
o: That is the definition of full-duplex.
The statement is true. Taking turns would be half-duplex; full-duplex is both at once.

questions.p: In which mode is the channel capacity shared by both directions at all times?
o: Simplex only uses one direction, so nothing is shared between directions.
Multipoint is a connection type (many devices on a link), not a data-flow mode.
Both directions are active at once, so the capacity is split between them all the time.
In half-duplex the sender gets the whole channel while it transmits; the directions take turns.

questions.p: A walkie-talkie is an example of:
o: Simplex would mean only one side could ever talk.
In full-duplex both talk at once, like a phone call.
Multiplexing combines several signals on one link; it isn’t a data-flow mode.
Both can talk, but only one at a time, which is why you say “over”.

questions.p: A keyboard sends data to a computer, and the computer never sends anything back on that channel. This is:
o: It may be point-to-point too, but the question asks about the direction of flow.
Half-duplex allows both directions, one at a time.
Full-duplex allows both directions at once.

questions.p: In half-duplex mode, the station that is sending uses the entire capacity of the channel.
o: Because the directions take turns, the sender has the whole channel while it transmits.
The statement is true. Sharing capacity between directions happens in full-duplex, not half-duplex.

questions.p: Topology describes:
o: The direction data flows on a link
That is simplex, half-duplex or full-duplex.
The rules devices follow to communicate
How far a network reaches geographically
How a network is physically laid out and how devices interconnect

questions.p: Which of these is NOT one of the four basic topologies?
o: Mesh is one of the four.
Ring is one of the four.
Bus is one of the four.
The four basic topologies are mesh, star, bus and ring.

questions.p: How many links are needed for a fully connected mesh of 6 devices?
o: 6 links would be a ring or a star.
6 x 5 = 30 counts every link twice. Divide by 2.
5 is the number of ports each device needs (N-1), not the number of links.

questions.p: In a mesh of 10 devices, how many I/O ports does each device need?
o: Each device connects to every other device: N-1 = 9 ports.
A device doesn’t need a port to connect to itself, so it is N-1.
45 is the total number of links, not ports per device.
90 is N(N-1), which counts each link twice.

questions.p: A mesh topology has no traffic (congestion) problems because each link is dedicated.
o: Each link carries only the traffic between its two devices, so devices don’t compete for links.
The statement is true: dedicated links mean no sharing, so no traffic problems between devices.

questions.p: Why is a fully connected mesh expensive?
o: The number of cables and ports grows quickly as devices are added
N(N-1)/2 links and N-1 ports per device add up fast.
It needs terminators at both ends of the backbone
It needs repeaters in every device
It needs an expensive central switch
That describes the cost of a star.

questions.p: Which topology requires a central controller or hub?
o: A bus uses a shared backbone cable, not a central controller.
In a mesh, devices link directly to each other.
In a ring, each device links to its two neighbours.
Every device links only to the central hub or switch.

questions.p: In a star network, one employee’s cable is cut. What happens?
o: Only that employee’s computer loses its connection
Each device has its own link to the hub, so one broken link affects one device.
Traffic is rerouted through a neighbour
Star devices have no links to neighbours; only to the hub.
The signal goes the other way round
That happens when the hub fails, or in a bus when the backbone breaks.

questions.p: A star topology needs N links for N devices.
o: One link from each device to the hub.
The statement is true: one link per device, all going to the central device.

questions.p: In a bus topology, one break in the cable can stop all transmissions on the segment.
o: Every device shares the backbone, so a break stops the signal for everyone.
The statement is true. A break in the backbone stops all transmission, which is the bus’s main weakness.

questions.p: One main cable plus N drop lines describes:
o: Devices connect to a single backbone through drop lines and taps.
A star has N links to a central device.
A ring has N point-to-point links in a loop.

questions.p: Why is it hard to add devices to a bus network?
o: Each tap weakens the signal and the backbone has a limited length
There is a limit to how many devices one backbone can carry.
Every device must be given a repeater
Each new device needs N-1 new ports
The hub has no free ports

questions.p: A ring of 12 devices needs how many links?
o: Each device links to its two neighbours, and N devices form N links in the loop.
A chain of 12 devices has 11 links; closing the loop adds one more.
There is no extra link beyond N.

questions.p: Fault isolation is easy in a ring topology.
o: A device that stops receiving the signal knows the problem is just before it and can raise an alarm.
The statement is true: the slide lists easy fault isolation as an advantage of the ring.

questions.p: What is the main disadvantage of a simple ring?
o: It needs a very large number of links
That is mesh. A ring needs only N.
All devices depend on a central hub
One broken link or device can stop the whole ring
Data has to travel all the way round, so a break blocks it.
Every device hears every transmission at once

questions.p: What does the repeater in each ring device do?
o: Sends the signal to every device at once
Devices only connect to their neighbours.
Converts the signal to a different protocol
A repeater only regenerates the signal.
Stores frames until the hub is free
There is no hub in a ring.
Regenerates the signal and passes it to the next device
Data travels device to device, and each repeater boosts it on.

questions.p: A network has a central switch with three bus segments attached. Its topology is:
o: The segments are buses, but they hang off a central device.
The centre is a star, but the bus segments make it a mix.
It combines a star backbone with bus segments.

questions.p: A LAN typically covers an area larger than 2 miles in diameter.
o: Check the size: a LAN is local. Something larger than that, across a city, is a MAN.
A LAN covers a room, a building or a campus, no more than a few kilometres.

questions.p: A network spanning a whole city is a:
o: A WAN spans countries or continents.
A personal area network covers about a metre around one person.
A LAN covers a building or campus.
Metropolitan area network: a town or a city.

questions.p: A university links the buildings on one campus. This is a:
o: A campus is the upper end of a LAN’s range.
The Internet is the worldwide internetwork.
A MAN covers a whole city.

questions.p: How do today’s LANs differ from the LANs in the figure’s “past” picture?
o: Today’s LANs connect hosts with a mesh
A mesh would need far too many cables.
Past LANs had no cables at all
Past LANs used one shared cable.
Each host has its own link to a switch instead of sharing one cable
The past LAN was a shared bus; today’s is a switched star.
Today’s LANs use a ring instead of a star

questions.p: A telecom company runs a network that links the LANs of several branches across one city. This is a:
o: A PAN is a few metres.
A LAN is a single building or campus.
City-wide, linking LANs, run by a telecom company.
A WAN would span countries or continents.

questions.p: In the two-building LAN, which device connects the whole LAN to the Internet?
o: The backbone links the building switches together, still inside the LAN.
A router connects one network to another.
Switches connect devices inside the LAN.

questions.p: An internet (lowercase i) is the same as the Internet (uppercase I).
o: Check the capital letter: “internet” is general (any internetwork), “Internet” is the one global network.
An internet is any set of connected networks; the Internet is one specific worldwide internet.

questions.p: Two LANs joined by routers over a WAN link form:
o: The Internet is the global one; this is a small private internet.
A MAN is classified by city size, not by joining networks.
Two or more connected networks make an internetwork.
They are still separate networks joined by routers.

questions.p: In a heterogeneous network made of LANs and WAN links, where are the routers?
o: At every point where two networks meet
Routers move data between networks, so they sit at each boundary.
Nowhere: WAN links connect LANs directly
A router is needed to pass data from one network to another.
Inside a LAN, switches connect devices.
Only at the end user’s computer
A host is not a router.

questions.p: What does a WAN provide?
o: Long-distance transmission between cities, countries or continents

questions.p: __ is the protocol suite of the current Internet.
o: ACM is a professional computing society, not a protocol suite.
All networks on the Internet run the TCP/IP suite.
NCP was used on the ARPANET before TCP/IP replaced it.

questions.p: Which is NOT required for a host to be on the Internet?
o: Being able to send IP packets to other machines
Being connected through a tier-1 ISP directly
A host can reach the Internet through any ISP tier.

questions.p: STC and Mobily are examples of:
o: Tier 1 is international, such as AT&T or Lumen.
They are national providers connected to at least one tier-1 ISP.
An IXP is an exchange point, not an ISP.
Tier 3 buys service from national providers like STC.

questions.p: Tier-1 ISPs connect directly to other tier-1 ISPs.
o: Backbones own their links and connect to each other directly.
The statement is true: tier-1 ISPs are connected directly to each other.

questions.p: A local ISP that buys its Internet access from a national provider is:
o: Tier 1 owns international links and buys from no one.
Tier 3 takes service from the national (tier-2) providers.
An IXP is where ISPs exchange traffic.
Tier 2 is the national provider itself.

questions.p: Which describes a tier-1 ISP?
o: Local coverage, buys service from national providers
International coverage, owns its links, connects directly to other tier-1s
Those are the backbone features on the slide.
National coverage, connected to at least one tier-1 ISP
A third-party switching facility where ISPs meet

questions.p: Lumen’s map shows links on every continent. What does this show about a tier-1 ISP?
o: It owns international infrastructure and can reach other networks without buying transit
Owning global links is what makes it a backbone.
It is an Internet Exchange Point
An IXP is a meeting point, not a global network.
It is a local ISP that serves one city
It depends on a national provider for access

questions.p: In the Internet structure, what is the access network?
o: The last hop that connects end systems to their local ISP
It is the link between your device or home and the ISP.
That is where ISPs exchange traffic.

questions.p: In the figure of the Internet today, where are the backbones joined to each other?
o: The access network is the last hop to end users.

questions.p: An Internet Exchange Point (IXP) is managed by:
o: That would make it private peering.
Public peering at an IXP is run by a neutral third party.

questions.p: National ISPs usually interconnect using IXPs.
o: The current trend: international ISPs use private peering, national ISPs use IXPs.
The statement is true. Private peering is the trend for international ISPs; national ones meet at IXPs.

questions.p: Private peering points are:
o: Used only by local tier-3 ISPs
Owned and operated by the ISPs themselves
The ISPs connect directly using their own routers.
Open for any ISP to join

questions.p: What is peering?
o: Sharing one cable among many devices
Connecting a host to its local ISP
Interconnecting networks so they can exchange traffic
Peering is about interconnection, not encryption.

questions.p: Why does a country benefit from an IXP?
o: It assigns IP addresses to users
IXPs exchange traffic; they don’t assign addresses.
Local ISPs exchange traffic locally instead of sending it abroad and back
It is faster and cheaper to keep local traffic local.
It replaces the need for tier-1 ISPs
Traffic to other countries still needs the backbones.

questions.p: A protocol is defined as the structure or format of data.
o: The statement describes syntax only. A protocol is the whole set of rules: syntax, semantics and timing.
A protocol is a set of rules controlling data exchange; format (syntax) is only one part of it.

questions.p: A protocol is best defined as:
o: The physical path of a message
A set of rules controlling the exchange of data

questions.p: Why could IBM and DEC computers not communicate in the early 1970s without translation software?
o: Networks had not yet been invented
They had local networks; they just couldn’t talk to each other.
Each vendor used its own networking architecture
There were no shared standards, so each vendor’s rules were different.
The problem was the rules, not the cables.

questions.p: The main reason standards are needed is:
o: To make each vendor’s equipment unique
That is the problem standards solve.
Interoperability between equipment from different vendors
Standards let products from different makers work together.
To increase the price of equipment
A large market usually lowers prices.

questions.p: “How many volts make a 0 and a 1?” and “how do we find a route to a machine?” show that:
o: Agreements are needed at many different levels
The list runs from electrical signals up to applications, which later become layers.
Standards are only needed for applications
Only the physical level needs a standard
Routing and applications need agreements too.
Each vendor should decide these for itself

questions.p: Which organization specializes in LAN/MAN standards?
o: ANSI is the US national standards body.
ITU-T is the UN telecommunications agency.
IEEE writes the 802 family: 802.3 Ethernet, 802.11 Wi-Fi.

questions.p: Which standards body is a United Nations agency?
o: ISO is international but not a UN agency.
The International Telecommunication Union is a UN agency.
IEEE is a professional engineering organisation.

questions.p: Which organisation sets the standards for the World Wide Web?
o: ISO is the general international standards body.
IEEE covers LAN and MAN standards.

questions.p: The boundary between two adjacent layers is called a(n):
o: A protocol is the set of rules between peer layers on different machines.
Peers are the same layer on two different machines.
A header is control information added to a PDU.
The interface defines what the lower layer offers the layer above.

questions.p: In a layered architecture, layer n-1 provides a service to layer n.
o: Each layer serves the layer directly above it.
The statement is true: the lower layer (n-1) serves the upper one (n), not the other way round.

questions.p: Why are network functions designed as layers?
o: To break a complex system into simpler, logically grouped parts
Layers are logical groupings of functions that make the complexity manageable.
Layering is about organisation, not speed.
So that each layer can talk directly to every other layer
A layer only talks to the layers directly above and below it.
To remove the need for protocols
Each layer has its own protocols.

questions.p: Rules used between the same layer on two different hosts are a:
o: An interface is between adjacent layers on the same host.
A protocol governs communication between peers at the same layer.
A service is what a layer offers the layer above it on the same host.
Topology is the physical layout of the network.

questions.p: Layer 3 on host 1 sends its data directly across the medium to layer 3 on host 2.
o: The communication between peers is logical. The real path goes down the stack, across the medium at layer 1, and up the other side.
Only layer 1 touches the medium. Layer 3’s data goes down to layer 1, across, and back up.

questions.p: Up to which layer does a router operate?
o: Routers don’t read transport headers; only hosts do.
That is as far as a switch goes.
A router uses layers 1 to 3, reading the IP address to pick the next network.
Only hosts use the application layer.

questions.p: A link-layer switch uses which layers?
o: It reads MAC addresses in frames, which is layer 2.
A switch never looks at IP or port numbers.
That would be a repeater or hub.

questions.p: Which device is the most complex in terms of layers?
o: A host implements all five layers.
A repeater implements only the physical layer.

questions.p: Why can a NIC from one company work with an operating system from another?
o: Both companies must share their source code
They only need to agree on the interface.
The application layer translates between them
Translation between data formats is the presentation layer’s job, and it isn’t what makes the parts fit.
The NIC implements every layer itself
The NIC only covers layers 1 and 2.
Each layer is implemented independently and respects the interface between layers
The fixed interface is what lets layers from different vendors fit together.

questions.p: The set of protocols used by all the layers is called:
o: An interface is the boundary between two adjacent layers.
The protocols are stacked like the layers.
A PDU is a unit of data at one layer.

questions.p: Which two standard protocol models does the slide name?
o: These are standards organisations, not models.
These are the two standard stacks.
These are network types by size.

questions.p: The OSI model was developed by:
o: ANSI is the US standards body.

questions.p: What is an “open system” in the OSI sense?
o: A set of protocols that lets any two systems communicate regardless of their architecture
A network that anyone can join without an address
A system whose source code is free
That is open source, a different idea.

questions.p: Which OSI layer number is the transport layer?
o: Layer 2 is the data link layer.
Counting from the bottom: physical 1, data link 2, network 3, transport 4.

questions.p: Which layer sits directly above the network layer in OSI?
o: Data link is below the network layer.

questions.p: Which OSI layer is number 6?
In “All People Seem To Need Data Processing”, what does the “S” stand for?
o: Segment is a PDU name, not a layer.
Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data link, Physical.

questions.p: Which layers are implemented in hardware on the NIC?
o: Network is mixed and transport is software.
The NIC builds frames and sends signals.

questions.p: The network layer is implemented in a mix of hardware and software.
o: The slide calls it a mixed implementation.
The statement is true. The top four layers are software, the bottom two hardware, and the network layer is in between.

questions.p: The transport layer is implemented in:
o: Only the physical and data link layers are on the NIC.
Application, presentation, session and transport are all software.
The cable is the medium, not a layer implementation.
A mix of hardware and software

questions.p: Which layers communicate end to end, without the intermediate nodes taking part?
o: These talk hop by hop with every node on the path.
Routers in between use only layers 1 to 3.
Intermediate nodes only have layers 1 to 3.

questions.p: Peers are:
o: Processes at the same layer on different machines
That is the definition of peers.
Adjacent layers on the same machine
Two hosts on the same LAN

questions.p: Which layer adds both a header and a trailer?
o: It adds a trailer with the error-detection code.
Physical adds no header; it sends bits.

questions.p: The header added by the transport layer is read by the receiver’s transport layer only.
o: Control information is read only by the peer layer.
The statement is true: each header is read and acted on only by its peer layer on the receiving node.

questions.p: A PDU consists of:
o: The data from the layer above plus the current layer’s control information
Payload plus header (and trailer at layer 2).
The PDU also carries the data from above.
The raw bits on the medium
That is only the physical layer’s view.
All headers from every layer below
Lower layers add their headers after this PDU is built.

questions.p: In the OSI exchange figure, which headers does the data link layer treat as plain data?
o: It carries all the upper headers, not only H7.
H7 down to H3, together with D7
Everything handed down from above is just data to the layer below.
Each layer reads only its own header.

questions.p: Data encapsulation means that layer N-1:
o: That is decapsulation at the receiver.
Only the peer layer reads a header.
Carries layer N’s PDU in its data part without knowing its contents
The lower layer wraps the upper PDU like a sealed letter.

questions.p: During encapsulation, a lower layer inspects and changes the upper layer’s header.
o: A lower layer treats the upper PDU as data. It never reads or changes the upper header.
It carries the upper PDU untouched.

questions.p: A frame is equal to:
o: A segment plus an IP header
A stream of bits with no headers
That is what the physical layer sends.
A message plus a TCP header
A packet plus the data link header and trailer
PDU(N-1) = PDU(N) + control information of N-1.

questions.p: What does each layer do during decapsulation?
o: Adds a new header and passes it down
That is encapsulation at the sender.
Removes its own header (and trailer) and passes the rest up
It undoes what its peer added.
Each layer removes only its own.
Sends the data back to the sender

questions.p: In TCP/IP, which layer does the job of OSI’s application, presentation and session layers?
o: TCP/IP merges OSI’s top three into one application layer.
TCP/IP has no separate session layer.

questions.p: What does the TCP header carry that identifies the receiving application?
o: That identifies the host; it is in the IP header.
That identifies the next device; it is in the frame header.

questions.p: The IP header added by the network layer contains:
o: The source and destination IP addresses
These identify the sending and final destination hosts.
The trailer is added by the data link layer.
The source and destination MAC addresses
Those are in the frame header.
The source and destination port numbers
Those are in the TCP header.

questions.p: The destination MAC address in the sender’s Ethernet frame is the address of:
o: That is the source MAC address.
DNS has nothing to do with frame addressing.
The next device on the link
MAC addresses only reach across one link.
Only if it is on the same link; otherwise it is the next hop.

questions.p: What does the receiving data link layer do if the destination MAC address is not its own (and not broadcast)?
o: It changes the address to its own
Addresses are not rewritten like that.
It sends it back to the sender
There is no return in that case.
It passes it up to the network layer anyway
The frame is filtered at layer 2.
The frame isn’t meant for this device.

questions.p: How does the receiving network layer know the packet has reached its destination?
o: Every Ethernet frame has a trailer.
The destination MAC matches its own
That check happens at the data link layer, at every hop.
The destination IP address in the header is its own
It compares the destination IP with its own address.
Ports are read by the transport layer.

questions.p: Which address does the receiving transport layer use to choose the application?
o: Sequence numbers put segments in order.
The IP address identifies the host, not the process.
Each process is identified by its port.
The MAC address identifies the network card.

questions.p: On the wire, the order of headers in front of the data is:
o: That is the order they are added, which puts TCP innermost.
The lowest layer’s header is added last, so it is outermost.
IP (layer 3) wraps TCP (layer 4), so IP comes first.

questions.p: The physical layer is responsible for moving:
o: Individual bits from one hop to the next
That is the physical layer’s definition.
That is the data link layer.

questions.p: Which device operates only at the physical layer?
o: A gateway can work at all layers.

questions.p: Data rate (bits per second) is defined by the physical layer.
o: The slide lists data rate among the physical layer’s duties.
The statement is true: the physical layer sets how many bits are sent per second.

questions.p: Making sure the sender’s and receiver’s clocks agree so each bit is read at the right time is:
o: Flow control stops a fast sender from flooding a slow receiver.
Dialog control is about who sends when.
The slide lists synchronisation of bits under the physical layer.

questions.p: The shape of a connector and the number of its pins are defined by which layer?
o: Physical characteristics of interfaces belong to layer 1.
Data link handles frames and MAC addresses.
Network handles IP addresses and routing.

questions.p: The RJ-45 connector is an example of something specified by which layer?
o: Data link defines frames, not plugs.

questions.p: The PDU of the data link layer is the:
Host A sends to host B through one router. The destination MAC address in A’s frame is:
o: The frame is addressed to one device.
B is on a different link; the frame can only reach the router.

One parity bit for the whole block

Four errors at the corners of a rectangle

questions.p: A channel of R = 10 Mbps is shared equally by M = 5 stations. What is R/M?

questions.p: Which is an example of a broadcast (shared) link?

Many nodes share the same radio channel.

questions.p: What is a collision?
o: A frame arriving out of order
Two or more frames on the shared medium at the same time, destroying each other
A frame with a wrong address

LLC handles error and flow control.
The network layer isn’t a sublayer.

questions.p: The MAC sublayer is responsible for:

Two may decide at the same moment.
A primary station schedules them badly

questions.p: In CSMA, a station senses the medium:

B’s signal hadn’t reached C yet because of propagation delay

The size of the jam signal
